analysis.investment_thesis: Alembic Pharmaceuticals is a century-old business with ten consecutive years of positive earnings, but at P/E 23.2x and P/B 2.9x it trades nearly double my maximum tolerable valuation. The Graham Number (~INR 425) implies the market is asking me to pay an 85% premium over intrinsic asset-earning value — a bargain hunter's nightmare.
key_strengths: Unbroken 10-year earnings record (2016–2025) with profits ranging INR 342–1,146 Cr — the minimum consistency I demand
Conservative balance sheet: D/E of 0.28 is well below my 0.5 ceiling, and borrowings were restrained until 2025
High promoter holding (69.74%) aligns management with long-term ownership, not short-term stock games
key_risks: Valuation grotesquely exceeds Graham Number: price INR 785 vs. computed Graham Number ~INR 425 (EPS ~29.6, BVPS ~271) — an 85% premium with zero margin of safety
Deteriorating earning power: 9-year Net Profit CAGR is -2.3% and EBITDA CAGR is -0.3% — revenue grows but profits shrink, the classic margin compression trap
Cash flow collapse in FY2025: OCF plunged from INR 803 Cr to just INR 88 Cr; FCF turned deeply negative (-INR 466 Cr); borrowings nearly tripled from INR 513 Cr to INR 1,489 Cr in a single year
red_flags: FY2025 OCF (INR 88 Cr) is a fraction of reported net profit (INR 582 Cr) — earnings quality is suspect; cash is not following profits
Finance costs compounding at 35.9% CAGR (INR 5 Cr → INR 79 Cr) signal mounting debt servicing burden eating into earnings
CWIP rose sharply to INR 903 Cr in FY2025 alongside a debt surge — capital allocation is voracious with no demonstrated payoff in profits yet
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative yardstick I have prescribed, Alembic Pharmaceuticals fails the test of the intelligent investor. P/E of 23.2x is 55% above my absolute ceiling of 15x. P/B of 2.9x is nearly double my 1.5x limit. The computed Graham Number of approximately INR 425 (using FY2025 EPS of ~29.6 and book value per share of ~271) exposes that the market demands an 85% premium over the price I would consider fair. Mr. Market is feeling ebullient; I am not obliged to join him.

What troubles me more than the price is the trend in earning power — the true foundation of intrinsic value. Over nine years, revenue grew 8.6% annually while net profits actually *shrank* at -2.3% CAGR. The company is running faster to stand still. Worse, FY2025 delivered a severe warning: operating cash flow collapsed to INR 88 Cr against net profit of INR 582 Cr, free cash flow turned negative at -INR 466 Cr, and management nearly tripled borrowings in one year to fund a capex binge (INR 564 Cr capex, CWIP INR 903 Cr). When a company earns on paper but cannot convert that to cash, I grow deeply suspicious. I require a margin of safety before I invest; here I find only a margin of danger.
